candidate.note: A planet candidate from an automated search, not a confirmed planet. It needs review by people and follow-up observations; other things, such as a faint background binary, can look the same.

checks.name: snr
checks.reason: The dip stands 18 times above the noise over 16 events.

checks.name: odd_even
checks.reason: Alternate dips have matching depths (0.170% vs 0.158%), as expected for a planet.

checks.name: secondary_eclipse
checks.reason: Halfway round the orbit there is no significant dip, consistent with a planet.

checks.name: size
checks.reason: Dip depth 0.164% on a 1.10 R_sun star implies about 0.43 Jupiter radii (4.8 Earth radii), likely range 0.41-0.45. That is within the size range of planets.

checks.name: period_alias
checks.reason: The period holds up against P/2, 2P and 3P: P/2: dip at half phase 11% of the main one; 2P: shallowest group 85% of the rest; 3P: shallowest group 68% of the rest.

checks.name: momentum_dump
checks.reason: 0 of 16 dips coincide with a momentum dump and 2 more with quality-flagged cadences; the clean dips alone are 92% as deep as all of them, so the signal does not come from spacecraft events.

checks.name: sector_depth
checks.reason: The dip depth agrees between sectors (S35 1986±425, S62 1965±173, S63 1315±188 ppm; chance of this scatter 0.03).

checks.name: duration
checks.reason: The dip lasts 1.9 h; a planet crossing the middle of this star (density 1.21 solar, from TIC density) on a 4.651-day orbit would take about 3.0 h, so the length fits.

checks.name: single_sector
checks.reason: Not a single-sector signal: dips were seen in 3 sectors.

score_detail.formula: (0.40*S_snr + 0.20*S_transits + 0.25*S_checks + 0.15*S_brightness) * (0.8 if single-sector); each part = weight * S * factor

stand_in.name: TOI-4257.01
stand_in.note: This is TOI-4257.01, already a TESS Object of Interest (ExoFOP disposition FP). The live search would file it as already known; it is shown here as a stand-in because the 2026-09-26 search found no new candidate.

reasons: Gaia sees a single, well-behaved star (RUWE 0.869).
2 Gaia neighbours within 42″ could be bright enough to fake the dip.
The pixel check puts the dip on a neighbouring star.
LEO and TRICERATOPS have not been run on it yet.

pixels.reason: the light lost during the dip comes from 25.1″ away from the target (21σ), closest to Gaia DR3 5423774792624492928 (G=14.3)
